title: New lump in follow-up: suspected recurrence

header.contentArea: History taking for suspected local recurrence
guidelineVersions: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (published June 2015; last updated May 2025)
NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer (published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025)

related.why: The original surgery and adjuvant treatment this new finding follows
The examination technique now applied to this new finding

brief.setting: Breast follow-up clinic, eighteen months after initial treatment
brief.scenario: Ms Rachel Linford, 43, completed surgery, radiotherapy and is on ongoing endocrine therapy. She has noticed a new lump near her previous scar.
brief.task: Take a focused history to assess this new finding. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present and discuss next steps.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Take the new lump seriously without alarming her; a focused history plus a calm, clear plan for urgent further assessment.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Reassuring her prematurely that it's "probably scar tissue" before taking a proper history or arranging assessment.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Can you tell me about the lump you've noticed - when did you first feel it?"

flow: Onset, site and change over time of the lump
Associated symptoms (skin change, nipple change, pain)
Systemic symptoms (weight loss, bone pain, breathlessness)
At 6 minutes: present and discuss next steps

grid.label: Characterising the lump
grid.fail: Does not establish when the lump was noticed or whether it has changed.
grid.pass: Establishes onset, exact site relative to the scar, and whether it has grown.
grid.high: Also asks how it was found (self-examination vs incidental) and whether she has noticed anything similar before.

grid.label: Associated local symptoms
grid.fail: Does not ask about skin or nipple change.
grid.pass: Asks about skin changes, nipple change or discharge, and pain at the site.
grid.high: Asks specifically about symptoms that would suggest local invasion (skin tethering, ulceration) versus a simpler cause (fat necrosis, cyst).

grid.label: Systemic red flags
grid.fail: Does not screen for symptoms of metastatic disease.
grid.pass: Asks about unexplained weight loss, bone pain, breathlessness or persistent cough.
grid.high: Directly links these questions to why they matter (screening for possible spread) in a way that doesn't frighten the patient unnecessarily.

grid.label: Treatment history
grid.fail: Does not check adherence to or details of her ongoing endocrine therapy.
grid.pass: Checks she has continued her endocrine therapy as prescribed and asks about any missed doses or side effects prompting her to stop.
grid.high: Considers whether poor adherence, rather than treatment failure, could be a contributing factor, without being accusatory.

grid.label: Presentation of findings
grid.fail: Gives a diagnosis rather than a differential, or minimises the finding.
grid.pass: Summarises the history and states that recurrence must be excluded, alongside benign explanations such as fat necrosis or a cyst.
grid.high: Presents this clearly without alarming language, while being honest that recurrence is a genuine possibility that needs prompt assessment.

grid.label: Next steps
grid.fail: Offers reassurance with no plan for further assessment.
grid.pass: Arranges urgent triple assessment (examination, imaging, biopsy) via the appropriate rapid pathway.
grid.high: Explains this will be expedited given her history, and that it will be discussed at the breast MDT once results are available.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's probably just scar tissue from your surgery, nothing to worry about.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop. What's your assessment and plan?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd just review her again in a few months to see if it's changed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me about the lump - when did you first notice it, and has it changed since?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: About three weeks ago, near my scar, and it feels a bit firmer now.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any changes in the skin over it, or your nipple, or any pain?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No skin or nipple changes, no pain.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you noticed any unexplained weight loss, bone pain, or breathlessness?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: And have you been able to keep taking your hormone therapy as prescribed?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop. What's your assessment and plan?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A new, growing lump near the previous surgical site in someone with a breast cancer history needs recurrence excluded, alongside benign causes like fat necrosis. I'd arrange urgent triple assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Can you tell me about the lump - when did you notice it, has it changed, and how did you come across it?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I felt it myself about three weeks ago, and it seems slightly bigger now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any skin tethering, ulceration, nipple changes or pain over it?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No, the skin looks normal and there's no pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd also like to check for anything that might suggest it's spread elsewhere - any unexplained weight loss, bone pain, or breathlessness?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: And have you managed to keep taking your hormone tablets regularly, or have there been any gaps?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I've taken them every day without missing any.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop. What's your assessment and plan?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A new, growing lump near her scar, with no skin, nipple or systemic symptoms, and good treatment adherence, still needs recurrence actively excluded alongside benign causes like fat necrosis or a cyst - I wouldn't want to reassure her without assessment. I'll arrange urgent triple assessment and make sure this is expedited given her history, then discuss the results at the breast MDT.

failures.move: Reassuring the patient it's "probably scar tissue" before any assessment.
failures.consequence: Delays diagnosis if this is a recurrence, and undermines trust if it later turns out not to be benign.
Misses a clue to possible metastatic disease that would change the urgency and scope of investigation.

failures.move: Deferring assessment to a routine future review.
failures.consequence: A new lump in someone with a breast cancer history needs urgent, not routine, assessment.

failures.move: Not asking about skin or nipple change over the lump.
failures.consequence: Misses a sign that could suggest local invasion, changing the urgency of assessment.

failures.move: Not checking adherence to her ongoing endocrine therapy.
failures.consequence: Misses a modifiable contributing factor and a chance to address it sensitively.

recovery.line: I shouldn't have said that before we've had a proper look - let's make sure we assess this properly first.

recovery.when: You forgot to screen for systemic symptoms
recovery.line: I'd also like to check whether you've noticed anything else, like weight loss or bone pain.

knowledge.fact: A new or growing lump near a previous surgical site in a patient with a breast cancer history warrants urgent triple assessment to exclude local recurrence.
Fat necrosis can present as a new firm lump near a previous surgical or radiotherapy site and can mimic recurrence clinically, which is why assessment rather than reassurance alone is needed.
Systemic symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, bone pain or breathlessness in someone with a breast cancer history should prompt consideration of possible metastatic disease.

recall.think: Don't reassure before assessing; screen for red flags; check adherence.
recall.say: "This needs proper assessment, not assumed scar tissue."
do: Establish onset and change in the lump
Screen local and systemic red flags (skin/nipple, weight loss, bone pain, breathlessness); check adherence
Arrange urgent triple assessment rather than routine review

numbers.meaning: maximum wait for a suspected cancer pathway referral for a new lump with a cancer history

recall.trap: Reassuring her it's "probably scar tissue" before assessment.
recall.finish: Urgent triple assessment arranged; recurrence neither assumed nor dismissed.

partner.opening: Please take a history from this patient about a new lump she's noticed. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 43, eighteen months after treatment, on ongoing endocrine therapy which you take reliably. You noticed a new, slightly enlarging lump near your scar three weeks ago. No skin, nipple or systemic symptoms. You are anxious this might be a recurrence.

reveals.finding: Lump noticed three weeks ago, near the scar, seems slightly bigger.

reveals.trigger: Asks about skin/nipple change or pain
reveals.finding: No skin or nipple change, no pain.
No weight loss, bone pain or breathlessness.
Taking endocrine therapy daily without missed doses.
Say: "Please stop there and tell me your assessment and plan."

push.question: Do you think it's come back?
push.expect: Be honest that recurrence needs to be excluded without asserting it is or isn't recurrence before assessment.

push.question: How quickly can I be seen?
push.expect: State this will be arranged urgently given her history, not deferred to routine follow-up.

curveballs.prompt: I've also had a persistent cough for two weeks.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Take this seriously as a possible systemic red flag, ask further questions, and ensure it's flagged as part of the urgent assessment rather than treated as unrelated.

curveballs.prompt: I stopped the hormone tablets a few months ago because of side effects, but didn't mention it before.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge this without judgement, note it as relevant history, and ensure it's communicated as part of the assessment rather than omitted.
